title: The mosques are for Allah
hookLine: the places of prostration belong to Allah, so call on none beside Him (72:18)
last: IT GUIDES TO WHAT IS RIGHT.

lines: A RUG IN AN AIRPORT CORNER.
IS ALL OF THAT A MOSQUE?
cards: A prayer rug unrolled in an airport corner, between a charging station and a newsstand. A man at a gas station, praying on a flattened cardboard box. A grandmother on her bedroom carpet.
A crowd of thousands, shoulder to shoulder, in a stone courtyard. Are all of those mosques? The English word mosque makes us think of a building with a dome.
The Arabic word underneath it is much smaller, and much bigger, and a verse in surah al-Jinn uses it.

teach.b: Verse eighteen, in Pickthall's translation: "And the places of worship are only for Allah, so pray not unto anyone along with Allah." The Arabic for places of worship is al-masajid.

One is a masjid, and the English word mosque comes from it. Masjid means a place of sujud, of prostration, where the forehead touches the ground: first of all, a spot where someone bows all the way down.
The commentators read this verse in more than one way.
Many say it means the mosque buildings: they belong to Allah, so in them, worship Him alone.
Others point to a hadith in Bukhari about the seven body parts a person prostrates on, forehead, hands, knees, feet: those, they say, are the masajid of the verse.

teach.h: THE SEVEN POINTS THAT TOUCH GROUND.
teach.b: Your own body's points of contact with the ground belong to Allah.

teach.h: THE WHOLE EARTH, A PLACE TO PRAY.
teach.b: And a third hadith widens it all: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said the whole earth has been made a masjid for him and his community, and pure. Wherever the time for prayer finds you, you can pray there.
That's why the airport corner and the cardboard box count. So the verse cuts two ways. It makes the humblest spot a place of worship.
And it makes even the grandest mosque nobody's property: not a ruler's, not a group's, not a builder's. In them, the verse says, call on no one alongside Him.
A masjid is defined less by its walls than by what happens on its floor.

how: Muslims pray in mosques and also wherever the time for prayer finds them, on any clean ground, often on a prayer rug; the mosque is treated as belonging to Allah, a place where worship is directed to Him alone.

o: a domed building with a tall minaret beside it
a school where children learn the Qur'an
a place of prostration, where foreheads touch ground

games.q: the time for prayer arrives while you're in an airport. there's no mosque. by the hadith, what can you do?
o: wait until you reach a mosque.
games.why: the earth was made a masjid, and pure: a clean corner, a rug, even cardboard, can be a place of prayer.

practice: If you can, clear a small space in front of you, a cloth, a rug, a patch of floor, and make it clean. If you pray, it's a spot you could pray on; if you don't, simply sit facing it.
Notice how a little clearing and cleaning turns ordinary floor into somewhere you'd put your forehead.

wordCard.voice: Masjid. In 72:18 the masajid, places of prostration, belong to Allah alone, from grand buildings to a clean patch of earth. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: places of prostration; singular masjid, the source of the English word mosque.
